title: Planetary motion and Kepler's laws
competency: State Kepler's three laws and use T²/R³ = K to solve orbit problems.

The point of an orbit nearest the Sun. The planet is fastest there.
The point of an orbit farthest from the Sun. The planet is slowest there.
The time for one complete revolution around the Sun (or another central body).

en.text: Kepler used Tycho Brahe's data on Mars. First law: every planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. Second law: the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, so a planet is fastest at perihelion (nearest the Sun) and slowest at aphelion (farthest).

screens.title: Earth's speed
screens.ask: Does Earth move round the Sun at the same speed all year?
opts: No, it is fastest when closest to the Sun
No, it is fastest when farthest
screens.after:
Earth speeds up as it nears the Sun and slows as it moves away.
The Sun–Earth line sweeps equal areas in equal times (Kepler's second law).
Near the Sun the line is short, so Earth must move faster.
screens.best: No, it is fastest when closest to the Sun

screens.title: From Ptolemy to Kepler
paras: Ptolemy (c.100–c.170): Earth at the centre (geocentric). Accepted for 1400 years.
Copernicus (1543): planets go round the Sun (heliocentric).
Tycho Brahe (1546–1601): careful positions of planets, without a telescope.
Kepler studied Brahe's data on Mars for 16 years and found three laws.

screens.title: First and second laws
paras: First law: the orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.
For every point on an ellipse, r₁ + r₂ is the same.
The other focus and the centre are empty.
Second law: the Sun–planet line sweeps equal areas in equal times.
So the planet is fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion.

screens.text: Kepler's first law: where is the Sun in a planet's orbit?
opts: At one focus of the ellipse
At the centre of the ellipse
screens.ans: At one focus of the ellipse
screens.why:
The orbit is an ellipse.
An ellipse has two foci.
The Sun sits at one focus.
The centre and the other focus are empty.
screens.clue: The ellipse has two special points.

screens.text: Kepler's second law, true or false: a satellite speeds up as it approaches the Sun and slows down as it moves away.
screens.why:
The Sun–planet line sweeps equal areas in equal times.
Near the Sun the line is short.
To sweep the same area, the planet must cover a longer arc.
So it moves faster near the Sun: true.

screens.title: Put the astronomers in time order
screens.why:
Ptolemy: about 100–170 (Earth at the centre).
Copernicus: 1543 (Sun at the centre).
Tycho Brahe: 1546–1601 (careful measurements).
Kepler: used Brahe's data to find his three laws.
screens.text: History of astronomy: put the astronomers in time order, oldest first.
screens.worked: Ptolemy → Copernicus → Tycho Brahe → Johannes Kepler.

screens.text: Circle and ellipse: how does a circle differ from an ellipse?
opts: A circle is an ellipse whose two foci are at the same point
A circle has two foci far apart
screens.ans: A circle is an ellipse whose two foci are at the same point
screens.why:
For an ellipse, r₁ + r₂ to the two foci is the same for every point.
Move the two foci together into one point.
Then every point is the same distance from it: a circle.
So a circle is an ellipse with both foci at one point.

screens.ask: Kepler's second law: at aphelion a planet is twice as far from the Sun as at perihelion. Its speed at perihelion is ___ times its speed at aphelion
screens.why:
At perihelion and aphelion the velocity is at 90° to r.
Area swept per second there = ½rv.
Equal areas: ½rₚvₚ = ½rₐvₐ.
vₚ/vₐ = rₐ/rₚ = 2.
screens.clue: Equal areas: a thin wedge far away must match a wide wedge near the Sun.

en.text: Kepler's third law compares planets: T²/R³ is the same constant K for every planet around the Sun (K ≈ 2.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ s²/m³). So T grows as R^(3/2): doubling R multiplies T by 2√2. Bodies orbiting a different central body (moons of Earth or Saturn) have their own constant.

am.text: የኬፕለር ሦስተኛ ሕግ፡ T²/R³ ለሁሉም የፀሐይ ፕላኔቶች አንድ ቋሚ ነው። R ሲጨምር T በፍጥነት ይጨምራል።

screens.title: Farther means slower
screens.ask: Move a planet farther from the Sun. How many times longer is its year?
screens.note: T₂/T₁ = (R₂/R₁)^(3/2). 4 times farther: 8 times longer. Mercury 88 days, Earth 365, Saturn 10 759.

screens.title: The law of periods
paras: The period T is the time for one complete orbit.
T²/R³ = K, the same for every planet of the Sun.
K does not depend on the planet's mass.
It holds for circles and ellipses (R = average distance).

screens.title: Check T²/R³ for real planets
screens.text: Tap a planet. R in Earth distances (AU), T in Earth years.

screens.title: Comparing two planets
steps: Saturn is 9 times farther than Earth: T = 1 × 9^(3/2) = 27 years.

screens.title: Key word
defs: The time for one complete revolution around the Sun (or another central body).

screens.text: Kepler's third law: if the radius of a circular orbit doubles, the period
screens.why:
Law: T² ∝ R³, so T ∝ R^(3/2).
R × 2 gives T × 2^(3/2).
2^(3/2) = 2√2 ≈ 2.83.
Trap: "×2" treats T as proportional to R.

screens.text: Kepler's third law: which has the shorter orbital period?
screens.why:
T² ∝ R³: closer planets have shorter years.
Earth is much closer to the Sun than Pluto.
Earth: 1 year. Pluto: about 248 years.
The planet's mass does not matter.

screens.ask: Kepler's third law: Saturn is 9 times farther from the Sun than Earth. Its period is ___ Earth years
screens.why:
Law: T₂/T₁ = (R₂/R₁)^(3/2).
T₂² = T₁² × 9³ = 1 × 729.
T₂ = √729 = 27 years.
Trap: 9 × 1 = 9 years ignores the powers.

screens.ask: Kepler's third law: Pluto is 39.44 times farther from the Sun than Earth. Its period ≈ ___ Earth years (nearest year)
screens.why:
Law: T = 1 year × (39.44)^(3/2).
√39.44 = 6.28.
T = 39.44 × 6.28 = 247.7 years.
Result: ≈ 248 years (≈ 9.0 × 10⁴ days; the book prints 10¹⁴).

screens.ask: Kepler's third law for moons: Titan orbits Saturn at 1.22 × 10⁹ m every 15.95 days. Hyperion orbits Saturn at 1.48 × 10⁹ m. Its period ≈ ___ days (1 decimal place)
screens.why:
Both orbit Saturn, so they share the same K.
T₂ = T₁ × (R₂/R₁)^(3/2).
R₂/R₁ = 1.48 ÷ 1.22 = 1.213; 1.213^(3/2) = 1.336.
T₂ = 15.95 × 1.336 ≈ 21.3 days.
screens.clue: Both orbit Saturn, so they share the same K.

screens.ask: Kepler's third law for satellites: the Moon orbits Earth every 27.3 days at 3.84 × 10⁸ m. A satellite orbits 1500 km above Earth (radius 6380 km). Its period ≈ ___ hours (1 decimal place)
screens.why:
Radius from Earth's centre: r = 6380 + 1500 = 7880 km = 7.88 × 10⁶ m.
Ratio: r/R_Moon = 7.88 × 10⁶ ÷ 3.84 × 10⁸ = 0.0205.
T = 27.3 days × 0.0205^(3/2) = 27.3 × 0.00294 = 0.0803 days.
Convert: 0.0803 × 24 ≈ 1.9 h.
Trap: using 1500 km (the height) instead of 7880 km.
screens.clue: Measure r from Earth's centre, not from the surface.

test.text: Kepler's first law: a planet's orbit is
opts: an ellipse with the Sun at one focus
a circle with the Sun at the centre
an ellipse with the Sun at the centre
test.ans: an ellipse with the Sun at one focus
test.why:
Law of ellipses: each orbit is an ellipse.
The Sun is at one focus, not at the centre.

test.text: Kepler's second law: a planet moves fastest at
opts: the end of the minor axis
test.why:
Equal areas in equal times.
The planet is nearest the Sun at perihelion.
So it moves fastest there and slowest at aphelion.

test.ask: Kepler's third law: a planet's average distance is made 4 times larger. Its period becomes ___ times longer

test.text: The constant K: is K = T²/R³ for the Moon around Earth the same as for planets around the Sun?
opts: No, it depends on the central body
Yes, if the Moon is heavy
No, it depends on the Moon's mass
test.ans: No, it depends on the central body
test.why:
Newton's law gives K = 4π²/(GM).
M is the mass of the central body.
Earth's mass is not the Sun's mass.
So K depends on the central body.

test.ask: Kepler's third law: a planet of the Sun has a period of 8 Earth years. Its distance is ___ times Earth's
test.why:
T² ∝ R³, so R³ = T² (in years and Earth distances).
R³ = 8² = 64.
R = ∛64 = 4.

notes.text: Table 2.2: the unit of T²/R³ should be s²/m³ (the "s" is missing).
Example 2.18: 365 days must be squared. Correct answer ≈ 9.0 × 10⁴ days (≈ 248 years), not 9.0 × 10¹⁴ days. "daya" is a typo.
Example 2.19 asks for a "distance in Earth years"; it means the period (27 years). Real Saturn: 9.5 AU, 29.5 years.
The perihelion/aphelion speed ratio (challenge) is added; it uses equal areas at the ends of the orbit.
